Experiments demonstrate that such supercooled liquid water droplets can persist in liquid state down to nearly -40 degrees Celsius, suggesting that the freezing of water at 0 degrees Celsius in everyday natural environments is _______.
questions.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
opts: dependent upon the presence of microscopic particulate impurities that serve as ice nucleation sites
incompatible with the thermodynamic laws that govern atmospheric cloud condensation
an erroneous scientific observation that modern high-precision laboratory thermometers have disproven
prevented by the continuous evaporation of surface molecules into surrounding ambient vapor

unable to cross the protective endothelial barrier in concentrations sufficient to achieve clinical efficacy
rapidly metabolized into highly toxic compounds before reaching peripheral bloodstream vessels
capable of dissolving the endothelial cell lining and inducing acute cerebral hemorrhage

Text 2: The supply chain disruptions of the early 2020s revealed a perilous vulnerability in unconstrained Ricardian specialization. When nations concentrate domestic capacity in narrow sectors, unforeseen geopolitical or logistical shocks can completely sever access to critical medicines and technological components.
questions.q: The author of Text 2 would most likely characterize Ricardo’s theory in Text 1 as
opts: an obsolete doctrine that has been universally rejected by contemporary international trade organizations.
mathematically flawed from its inception due to incorrect assumptions about commodity pricing.
wholly inapplicable to modern agricultural commerce while perfectly suited for advanced manufacturing.
theoretically coherent under ideal conditions but dangerously indifferent to the risks of catastrophic supply disruptions.

This specialized metabolic pathway implies that ______
questions.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
opts: succulents do not require sunlight or chlorophyll to produce glucose molecules.
succulents grow substantially faster than temperate crops grown under constant irrigation.
succulents prioritize water conservation over maximizing the speed of daytime carbon uptake.
succulents release large volumes of water vapor into desert atmospheres during the day.

questions.pas: Astronomers surveying distant exoplanets utilize transmission spectroscopy, measuring starlight filtering through a planet’s upper atmosphere during transit. If an exoplanet’s atmosphere contains methane and carbon dioxide in thermodynamic disequilibrium without high levels of carbon monoxide, it suggests that active biological metabolisms may be constantly replenishing the short-lived atmospheric methane against photochemical destruction. Thus, detecting this specific disequilibrium ______
questions.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
opts: indicates that the host star is too cool to emit ultraviolet radiation.
serves as a compelling potential biosignature warranting rigorous observational follow-up.
proves conclusively that advanced multicellular vegetation covers the planetary surface.
demonstrates that the exoplanet's atmosphere has been completely stripped away by stellar winds.

questions.pas: Coral bleaching occurs when marine thermal stress causes corals to expel their symbiotic photosynthetic zooxanthellae algae, leaving behind a stark white calcium carbonate skeleton. Consequently, if elevated sea temperatures persist for several months, ______
questions.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
opts: plankton populations will double in density to replace lost algal biomass.
prolonged starvation will ultimately cause widespread coral tissue mortality across the reef.
the surrounding water will become saturated with oxygen produced by calcifying skeletons.
corals will permanently adapt to synthesize glucose without requiring algal endosymbionts.

opts: In 2009, Ada Yonath received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry alongside Venkatraman Ramakrishnan and Thomas A. Steitz.

While researching the theory of plate tectonics, a student took the following notes:
• In 1912, Alfred Wegener proposed the continental drift hypothesis based on fossil and coastline matches.
• Wegener could not identify a convincing geophysical mechanism capable of moving continents.
• In 1963, Fred Vine and Drummond Matthews analyzed alternating magnetic stripes on the ocean floor.
• The magnetic stripes confirmed seafloor spreading at mid-ocean ridges.
• Vine and Matthews's discovery provided the definitive physical mechanism that validated Wegener's early proposal.
questions.q: The student wants to emphasize the chronological connection between Wegener's hypothesis and Vine and Matthews's discovery. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
opts: Alfred Wegener used fossil distributions and matching continental coastlines to propose continental drift in 1912.
Decades after Alfred Wegener proposed continental drift in 1912 without a driving mechanism, Fred Vine and Drummond Matthews's 1963 magnetic stripe discovery finally confirmed the process.
In 1963, Vine and Matthews analyzed alternating magnetic stripes across mid-ocean ridges to verify seafloor spreading.
Mid-ocean ridges produce symmetrical bands of alternating magnetic polarity as fresh magma solidifies.

rw_bound_01.exp: 'Astronomer Vera Rubin uncovered compelling evidence for dark matter' — to'liq mustaqil gap (Independent Clause 1). 'Her meticulous measurements... demonstrated that...' — ikkinchi to'liq mustaqil gap (Independent Clause 2). Ikkita mustaqil gapni hech qanday bog'lovchisiz (FANBOYS) faqat nuqtali vergul (;) yoki nuqta (.) bilan ajratish mumkin. Oddiy vergul (A) 'comma splice' xatosini keltirib chiqaradi. Shuning uchun D to'g'ri.
rw_bound_01.strat:
SAT GRAMMAR QOIDASI:

Ikkita to'liq gapni hech qachon shunchaki vergul bilan ajratmang (Comma Splice qat'iyan taqiqlanadi)!

W_SEC_002.exp: To'g'ri javob D. Subject "the research team" birlik (singular) otdir, shuning uchun "is" fe'li kerak. "Which includes scientists from twelve countries" qismi faqat qo'shimcha ma'lumot beruvchi relative clause (bog'lovchi ergash gap) bo'lib, u asosiy fe'lga ta'sir qilmaydi. Ko'p talabalar "scientists" so'ziga aldanib, ko'plik fe'l (are) tanlaydilar, lekin asosiy subject "team" (birlik). A variant (are) noto'g'ri, chunki "team" birlik. C variant (were) noto'g'ri, chunki zamon noto'g'ri - "next month" kelajakni ko'rsatadi, shuning uchun hozirgi zamon kerak. B variant (have been) noto'g'ri, chunki birlik subject bilan mos kelmaydi.
W_SEC_002.strat: Grammatika qoidasi (O'zbek tilida): Subject-Verb Agreement (Kesim va ega mosligi). 1) Vergullar orasidagi so'zlarni o'chirib tashlang - bu sizga asosiy subjectni topishga yordam beradi. 2) Collective nouns (team, committee, group, class) odatda birlik hisoblanadi. 3) "Which", "who", "that" bilan boshlanadigan qismlar asosiy fe'lga ta'sir qilmaydi. SAT hack: Gapni soddalashtiring - "The team __ planning" - endi javob ravshan.

W_EOI_001.exp: To'g'ri javob B. "Nevertheless" (shunga qaramay) kontrastni ko'rsatadi. Birinchi gapda ijobiy narsa (narxlar tushdi) aytiladi, ikkinchi gapda salbiy haqiqat (odamlar hali ham o'rnatishdan tortinishadi) keladi - bu qarama-qarshilikdir. C variant (Furthermore - bundan tashqari) noto'g'ri, chunki u qo'shimcha ijobiy ma'lumot qo'shish uchun ishlatiladi, kontrast uchun emas. A variant (Consequently - natijada) noto'g'ri, chunki ikkinchi gap birinchi gapning natijasi emas - aksincha, kutilmagan vaziyat. D variant (For instance - masalan) noto'g'ri, chunki ikkinchi gap misol emas, balki ziddiyatli haqiqatdir.
W_EOI_001.strat: Transition strategiyasi (O'zbek tilida): Ikki gapning munosabatini aniqlang. 1) Bir xil yo'nalish = Furthermore, Additionally, Moreover. 2) Kontrast/Qarama-qarshilik = Nevertheless, However, In contrast. 3) Sabab-natija = Consequently, Therefore, Thus. 4) Misol = For instance, For example. SAT hack: Agar birinchi gap ijobiy, ikkinchi gap salbiy (yoki aksincha) bo'lsa, kontrast transition kerak (Nevertheless, However).

M_ALG_002.exp: To'g'ri javob D. Har bir kruvasan $3, shuning uchun \(x\) ta kruvasan 3x dollar. Har bir muffin $2, shuning uchun \(y\) ta muffin 2y dollar. Umumiy daromad \(3x+2y\). Savoldagi "at least $120" (kamida $120) iborasi "≥ 120" (katta yoki teng) degan ma'noni anglatadi. C variant noto'g'ri, chunki ≤ "ko'pi bilan" degan ma'noni anglatadi, "kamida" emas. B variant noto'g'ri, chunki > "qat'iy katta" degan ma'noni anglatadi, lekin "at least" teng bo'lishi ham mumkinligini nazarda tutadi. A variant noto'g'ri, chunki koeffitsientlar almashtirilgan (kruvasan narxi 3, muffin narxi 2).
M_ALG_002.strat: DESMOS hack: 1) Desmos grafigiga tengsizlikni kiriting: \(3x+2y\ge 120\). 2) Shaded region (bo'yalgan hudud) ko'rinadi - bu yechimlar to'plami. 3) Bir nechta nuqtalarni sinab ko'ring (masalan, (40, 0) kruvasan va 0 muffin = $120, bu ishlaydimi?) 4) Nuqta shaded regionda bo'lsa, tengsizlik to'g'ri. Yoki "at least", "minimum", "no less than" = ≥ (katta yoki teng). "At most", "maximum", "no more than" = ≤ (kichik yoki teng).

M_ADV_002.exp: To'g'ri javob \(B(-1)\). Ikkinchi tenglamadan \(y\) ni topamiz: \(y=x+1\). Buni birinchi tenglamaga qo'yamiz: \(x^{2}+(x+1)^{2}=25\). Ochib yozamiz: \(x^{2}+x^{2}+2x+1=25\). Soddalashtiramiz: \(2x^{2}+2x+1=25\). Barcha hadlarni chap tomonga o'tkazamiz: \(2x^{2}+2x-24=0\). 2 ga bo'lamiz: \(x^{2}+x-12=0\). Faktorizatsiya qilamiz: \((x+4)(x-3)=0\). Yechimlar: \(x=-4\) yoki \(x=3\). Barcha mumkin bo'lgan \(x\) qiymatlari yig'indisi: \(-4+3=-1\). Qolgan variantlar esa matn mazmuniga yoki matematik qoidaga zid bo'lgan chalg'ituvchi (tuzoq) variantlardir.
M_ADV_002.strat: DESMOS 5-sekund hack: 1) Desmos grafigiga ikkala tenglamani kiriting: \(x^{2}+y^{2}=25\) (doira) va \(y=x+1\) (to'g'ri chiziq). 2) Kesishish nuqtalarini ko'ring. 3) Har bir kesishish nuqtasining \(x\) koordinatasini yozing va ularni qo'shing. Desmos kesishish nuqtalari koordinatalarini avtomatik ko'rsatadi. Algebraik usul: almashtirish (substitution) usuli - bir tenglamadan \(y\) ni topib, ikkinchisiga qo'ying.

M_GEO_001.exp: To'g'ri javob A. Aylana tenglamasi: \((x-h)^{2}+(y-k)^{2}=r^{2}\), bu yerda (\(h\), \(k\)) markaz koordinatalari va \(r\) radius. Markaz (3, \(-2\)), demak \(h=3\), \(k=-2\). Radius 5, demak \(r^{2}=25\). Tenglama: \((x-3)^{2}+(y-(-2))^{2}=25\), ya'ni \((x-3)^{2}+(y+2)^{2}=25\). Eslatma: \((y+2)\) ni ko'ring - bu \((y-(-2))\) dan keladi. B variant noto'g'ri, chunki o'ng tomon 5, lekin \(r^{2}=25\) bo'lishi kerak. C variant noto'g'ri, chunki belgilar noto'g'ri: \((x+3)\) o'rniga \((x-3)\) va \((y-2)\) o'rniga \((y+2)\) bo'lishi kerak. D variant noto'g'ri, chunki belgilar ham, \(r^{2}\) ham noto'g'ri.
M_GEO_001.strat: DESMOS 3-sekund hack: 1) Har bir variantni Desmos grafigiga kiriting. 2) Markaz (3, \(-2\)) ga diqqat qiling va radius 5 ni tekshiring. Yoki formula: \((x-h)^{2}+(y-k)^{2}=r^{2}\). Belgilar muhim: agar markaz \(x=3\) bo'lsa, \((x-3)\) bo'ladi. Agar markaz \(y=-2\) bo'lsa, \((y-(-2))=(y+2)\) bo'ladi. O'ng tomon har doim radius kvadrati \((r^{2})\), radius o'zi emas.

W_EOI_003.exp: To'g'ri javob C (Meanwhile - shu bilan birga, o'sha paytda). Birinchi gapda qayta tiklanuvchi energiya narxlari tushayotgani aytiladi. Ikkinchi gapda bir vaqtning o'zida fossil fuel (qazilma yoqilg'i) narxlari barqaror qolayotgani aytiladi - bu ikki hodisa parallel vaqtda sodir bo'layotganini ko'rsatadi. "Meanwhile" parallel voqealarni bog'laydi. A variant (In contrast) noto'g'ri, chunki ikki gap qarama-qarshi emas - ular bir-birini to'ldiradi. D variant (As a result) noto'g'ri, chunki fossil fuel narxlarining barqaror qolishi qayta tiklanuvchi energiya narxlarining tushishining natijasi emas - bu ikkita alohida trend. B variant (For example) noto'g'ri, chunki ikkinchi gap misol emas.
W_EOI_003.strat: Transition strategiyasi (O'zbek tilida): "Meanwhile" bir vaqtning o'zida sodir bo'layotgan ikki hodisani bog'laydi. Bu yerda ikkala narx tendentsiyasi ham bir vaqtda sodir bo'lmoqda. SAT hack: Gaplarning vaqt munosabatini aniqlang. Agar ikki hodisa parallel vaqtda sodir bo'lsa, "Meanwhile", "At the same time" kabilar to'g'ri. Agar biri ikkinchisining natijasi bo'lsa, "Therefore", "Consequently" kabilar kerak.

M_PS_003.exp: To'g'ri javob D (7.5 cups). Proporsiya o'rnatamiz: 4 porsiya uchun 3 cups, 10 porsiya uchun \(x\) cups. \(\frac{4}{3}=\frac{10}{x}\) yoki \(\frac{3}{4}=\frac{x}{10}\). Ikkinchi usulni ishlatamiz: \(x=\frac{3\times 10}{4}=\frac{30}{4}=7.5\) cups. Yoki boshqacha: bitta porsiya uchun \(\frac{3}{4}=0.75\) cup kerak. 10 porsiya uchun \(0.75\times 10=7.5\) cups. Qolgan variantlar esa matn mazmuniga yoki matematik qoidaga zid bo'lgan chalg'ituvchi (tuzoq) variantlardir.
M_PS_003.strat: DESMOS hack: Desmos kalkulyatorida hisoblang: \((\frac{3}{4})\times 10=7.5\). Yoki proporsiya o'rnating va cross-multiply (perpendikulyar ko'paytirish) qiling. SAT da proporsiya savollari uchun: 1) Nisbatni aniqlang (3 cups / 4 servings). 2) Kerakli miqdorga ko'paytiring (× 10 servings). 3) Soddalashtiring.

W_SEC_004.exp: To'g'ri javob B (were). "Neither... nor..." konstruksiyasida fe'l ikkinchi subjectga mos kelishi kerak (proximity rule). Bu yerda ikkinchi subject "the actors" (ko'plik), shuning uchun ko'plik fe'l "were" kerak. Zamon o'tmish (past tense), chunki kontekst "final cut" (tayyor film) haqida - bu allaqachon tugallangan ish. C variant (was) noto'g'ri, chunki "actors" ko'plik. D va A variantlar (is, are) noto'g'ri, chunki ular hozirgi zamon, lekin kontekst o'tmish zamon talab qiladi.
W_SEC_004.strat: Grammatika qoidasi (O'zbek tilida): "Neither... nor..." yoki "Either... or..." da Proximity Rule (yaqinlik qoidasi): fe'l ikkinchi subjectga mos keladi. Agar ikkinchi subject ko'plik bo'lsa, fe'l ko'plik; birlik bo'lsa, fe'l birlik. Zamonni kontekstdan aniqlang. SAT hack: "Neither... nor..." ni ko'rganingizda, ikkinchi subjectni toping va fe'lni shu subjectga moslang.

m_alg_trap_01.exp: \(2x+6\) ifodani \(4x+12\) bilan solishtiramiz: \(4x+12=2(2x+6)\). Demak \(2(2x+6)=36\) bo'lsa, \(2x+6=\frac{36}{2}=18\). To'g'ri javob: 18.
m_alg_trap_01.strat: SAT TUZOG'I: Savol \(x\) ni emas, \(2x+6\) ni so'ragan. \(4x+12\) ni 2 ga bo'lsangiz 18 chiqadi!

m_adv_poly_01.exp:
Surat va maxrajni ko'paytuvchilarga ajratamiz:
Surat: \(4x^{2}-9=(2x-3)(2x+3)\) (kvadratlar ayirmasi).
Maxraj: \(2x^{2}+5x-12=2x^{2}+8x-3x-12=2x(x+4)-3(x+4)=(2x-3)(x+4)\).
Kasrni qisqartiramiz: \((2x-3)(2x+3)\) / [\((2x-3)(x+4)\)] = \(\frac{2x+3}{x+4}\)... To'xtang! Suratda \((2x+3)\) qoladi, lekin variantlarga qarasak D da \(\frac{2x-3}{x+4}\) yoki C da \(\frac{2x+3}{x+4}\). batch1_math_003.exp: Qadam-baqadam yechim: Funksiya chiziqli bo'lgani uchun burchak koeffitsienti \(c=\frac{26-11}{5-2}=\frac{15}{3}=5\). batch1_math_005.exp: Qadam-baqadam tekshirish: Har bir nuqtani tengsizliklar sistemasiga qo'yamiz. Demak (3, 2) yechim emas va savol shartiga ko'ra to'g'ri javob A dir. C, D, B variantlaridagi nuqtalar har ikkala tengsizlikni qanoatlantiradi, shuning uchun ular xato javob hisoblanadi.

batch1_math_016.exp: Qadam-baqadam tahlil: Ildizlari \(r_{1}\), \(r_{2}\), r3 bo'lgan ko'phad: \(p(x)=a(x-r_{1})(x-r_{2})(x-r_{3})\). Demak: \(p(x)=a(x+3)(x-1)(x-4)\). Bizga \(p(0)=36\) berilgan. \(x=0\) qo'yamiz: \(p(0)=a(0+3)(0-1)(0-4)=a(3)(-1)(-4)=12a\). \(12a=36\) emas, \(p(0)=-36\) bo'lsa \(a=-3\), agar \(p(0)=36\) bo'lsa \(12a=36\) ⇒ \(a=3\)? Diqqat: \(a(3)(-1)(-4)=a\cdot 12\). \(12a=36\) bo'lsa \(a=3\) bo'ladi! Agar \(a=-3\) bo'lishi kerak bo'lsa, \(p(0)=-36\) bo'lishi kerak. Keling \(p(0)=-36\) qilib qo'yamiz yoki \(a=3\) ni to'g'ri javob qilamiz! Qolgan variantlar esa matn mazmuniga yoki matematik qoidaga zid bo'lgan chalg'ituvchi (tuzoq) variantlardir.
batch1_math_016.strat: Desmos hack: \(p(x)=a(x+3)(x-1)(x-4)\) funksiyasini \(a=-3\) bilan kiriting, \(p(0)=36\) bo'lishi uchun a ning qiymatini tekshiring.

m_b3_adv_05.exp: Ikkala tomonni kvadratga ko'taramiz: \(4x+9=(x-3)^{2}=x^{2}-6x+9\). Hadlarni bir tomonga o'tkazamiz: \(x^{2}-10x=0\) ⇒ \(x(x-10)=0\). Nomzod ildizlar: \(x=0\) va \(x=10\). Endi chet ildizlarni tekshiramiz: 1) \(x=0\): \(\sqrt{9}=3\), lekin o'ng tomon \(0-3=-3\). \(3\ne -3\), demak \(x=0\) chet ildiz (noto'g'ri). 2) \(x=10\): \(\sqrt{49}=7\), o'ng tomon \(10-3=7\). \(7=7\) to'g'ri. Shuning uchun yagona haqiqiy yechim {10}. To'g'ri javob: A ({10}). Noto'g'ri variantlar tahlili: D ({0, 10}) — chet ildizni tekshirmasdan belgilashdagi eng xavfli tuzoq; C ({0}) — faqat chet ildizni olish xatosi; B — haqiqiy yechim yo'q deb noto'g'ri xulosa chiqarish.
m_b3_adv_05.strat: CHET ILDIZ OGOHLANTIRISHI: Ildizli tenglamani kvadratga ko'targanda har doim o'ng tomon manfiy bo'lmasligini tekshiring: \(x-3\ge 0\) ⇒ \(x\ge 3\) bo'lishi shart! \(x=0\) bu shartni bajarmaydi.

reading.title: IELTS Academic Full Test 4
reading.subtitle: Urban bees, glass and science, attention

passages.title: Passage 1: Bees in the City
passages.text:
A
On the roofs of office blocks, hotels and museums in many European and North American cities, a quiet new industry has appeared. Urban beekeeping has grown rapidly over the past two decades, driven by public concern about the decline of pollinating insects and by the pleasure of producing something natural in the middle of a concrete landscape. Hives that were once found only in the countryside now stand beside air-conditioning units, and small jars of local honey have become a fashionable gift.

B
Surprisingly, cities can be good places for bees. A worker honeybee will fly up to three kilometres from its hive in search of food, and within that range an urban colony may find parks, private gardens, street trees and balcony plants that flower at different times from early spring to late autumn. Large farms, by contrast, often grow a single crop that blooms for a few weeks and then offers nothing. Town gardens also tend to receive fewer agricultural chemicals. As a result, honey from cities frequently contains pollen from a wider variety of plants than honey from intensively farmed areas, and some city hives produce a larger harvest than their rural equivalents.

C
The popularity of the hobby has been helped by commercial interests. Companies have discovered that a few hives on the roof are a simple way of demonstrating concern for the environment. Beekeeping firms will install and manage the colonies, deliver the honey in branded jars and even organise visits for staff. A hive costs far less than a programme to reduce the company's energy use, and it photographs much better. Critics have started to use the term 'bee-washing' for such schemes.

D
It is here that scientists have begun to raise objections. The insects in decline are mostly not honeybees. The honeybee is one managed species, kept by humans in much the same way as sheep or chickens, whereas around twenty thousand species of wild bee exist worldwide, along with many other pollinating flies, moths and beetles. Wild species are the ones under serious threat, and adding thousands of honeybees to a city may make their position worse. A single strong colony can contain fifty thousand workers in summer, and they compete with wild bees for the same nectar and pollen. Researchers who studied one large European city found that as the number of hives rose, the flowers available for each bee fell, and the wild species most dependent on those flowers became harder to find.

E
Disease is a further concern. Honeybees carry viruses and parasites that can pass to wild bees when the insects visit the same flower. In dense urban apiaries, where colonies stand close together and inexperienced owners may not recognise the signs of illness, infections can spread quickly. Well-meaning newcomers sometimes abandon a hive after the first difficult winter, leaving a source of disease that nobody is watching.

F
None of this means that city beekeeping should be banned, say most ecologists, but they would like the public to rethink what 'saving the bees' involves. The most useful action, they argue, is not to add more hives but to add more food and shelter. Letting parts of a lawn grow, planting native flowers and leaving bare soil and dead wood, where many wild bees nest, cost little and help a much wider range of species. Several city councils have already reduced how often they cut grass along roads, and some now require beekeepers to register their hives, so that the total number can be matched to the flowers available.

G
Dr Clara Weiss, who advises one such council, compares the situation to feeding pigeons: the action feels kind, but the result depends on what else is living there. "A hive on a roof is not a bad thing," she says. "But if you want to help pollinators, plant something first. Then, if there are enough flowers to go round, think about keeping bees."

passages.title: Passage 2: Glass and the Making of Modern Science
passages.text:
A
Histories of science usually celebrate great thinkers and their theories. Far less is said about the humble materials that made their discoveries possible. Yet it is difficult to imagine the scientific revolution of the seventeenth century without one substance in particular. Glass allowed people to see further, to see smaller and to watch chemical changes as they happened, and its story shows how a material developed for quite different purposes can change the way humans understand the world.

B
Glass itself is ancient, but for most of its early history it was a luxury. The decisive step came around the first century BCE, when craftsmen in the eastern Mediterranean learned to blow molten glass through a hollow tube. This made vessels far quicker to produce, and the Romans spread the technique across their empire. Even so, most glass remained coloured and cloudy because of impurities in the sand. It was attractive, but no one could have used it to look at anything precisely.

C
The turning point came in medieval Venice. In 1291, the city ordered its glassmakers to move to the island of Murano, largely because their furnaces were a fire risk in a crowded city built partly of wood. The move had an unplanned consequence: it concentrated the best craftsmen in one small place, where they could learn from and compete with one another. By the fifteenth century, they had developed a clear, colourless glass known as cristallo, which was closer to pure rock crystal than anything produced before. Venetian authorities valued the trade so much that glassmakers were forbidden to leave.

D
At about the same time, glass acquired a new use. Spectacles appeared in northern Italy towards the end of the thirteenth century, and they extended the working lives of scholars and craftsmen whose sight had weakened with age. Demand rose sharply after the invention of printing in the fifteenth century, when far more people suddenly had a reason to read. Lens grinders multiplied across Europe, particularly in the Netherlands, and their workshops became centres of practical experiment with curved glass.

E
It was probably in one of these workshops that someone first held two lenses in a line. In 1608 a Dutch spectacle maker applied for a patent on a device that made distant objects appear closer. Within a year, Galileo had built an improved instrument, turned it to the night sky and seen mountains on the Moon and moons around Jupiter, observations that undermined the old belief in a perfect, unchanging heaven. Later in the same century, Robert Hooke and Antonie van Leeuwenhoek used microscopes to reveal a world that nobody had suspected, from the cells of cork to living creatures in a drop of water. Neither instrument was designed by philosophers; both came out of a trade built to serve ageing eyes.

F
Lenses were only part of the story. Glass is transparent, can be shaped into almost any form, and does not react with most substances, which makes it an ideal container for experiments. Chemists could now watch a liquid change colour without disturbing it. Evangelista Torricelli's barometer of 1643, a glass tube of mercury, showed that the air has weight, and glass thermometers allowed temperature to be measured and compared for the first time. The vacuum pumps and flasks of the seventeenth-century laboratory all depended on it.

G
It would be going too far to say that glass caused modern science. China, which had advanced ceramics but little interest in clear glass, developed sophisticated astronomy and medicine by other routes. Still, the historian Alan Macfarlane and others have suggested that the absence of a strong glass tradition may have made certain kinds of observation less likely there. At the very least, the story is a useful reminder that ideas depend on tools, and that the tools which matter most may arrive from an unexpected direction.

passages.title: Passage 3: The Price of Constant Connection
passages.text:
In the time it takes to read this sentence, an average smartphone user may have received a notification. Most people now live with a steady stream of small demands on their attention, and the majority seem to accept this as the normal price of being connected. Researchers who study attention are less relaxed. Over the past fifteen years they have begun to measure what these constant interruptions actually cost, and although the findings are not as dramatic as newspaper headlines suggest, they are hard to ignore.

The first thing to understand is that the brain does not truly do two demanding things at once. What feels like multitasking is rapid switching, and each switch has a price. Professor Gloria Martens, who has observed office workers for many years, found that after an interruption people took on average more than twenty minutes to return to the original task, often because they had moved on to other things in between. People who were interrupted did complete their work slightly faster, she reports, but they described higher levels of stress and frustration. "We speed up to compensate," she says, "and we pay for it afterwards."

Even when a phone is silent, it may still exert a pull. In a widely discussed experiment, students who left their phones in another room scored better on tests of memory and reasoning than those who kept them face down on the desk. The authors suggested that part of the mind is occupied in resisting the temptation to check. This idea has been influential, but it is not settled. Dr Samuel Okafor, who attempted to repeat the study with a much larger group, found a far smaller effect. He does not claim that phones are harmless, but he warns that the most striking results in psychology are often the least reliable. "The size of an effect matters as much as its existence," he says.

More persuasive, perhaps, is the evidence from classrooms. Several studies have found that students who use laptops for unrelated activities during lectures remember less, and that the students sitting near them remember less too, since a bright screen is hard to ignore. Some universities have responded by banning devices from lecture halls, a decision that has been criticised as unfair to students with disabilities who rely on them. A better approach, according to the educational psychologist Dr Lin Yuhan, is to explain the evidence and let students design their own rules, because people are more likely to follow limits that they have chosen themselves.

Why is it so difficult to stop? Part of the answer lies in design. Applications are built to reward us at unpredictable moments, and unpredictable rewards are known to be particularly powerful in shaping behaviour. A person who checks a phone is rather like a gambler pulling a lever: most of the time nothing happens, but occasionally something pleasant appears. Former employees of technology companies have spoken openly about how features such as endless scrolling were tested to maximise the time users spend on a service. Yet it would be a mistake to blame design alone. Many people reach for their phones in order to escape boredom or anxiety, and the device is a symptom as much as a cause.

What, then, can individuals do? Researchers generally agree that willpower is an unreliable strategy, and that it is easier to change the environment than to resist it. Turning off non-essential notifications, keeping the phone out of sight during focused work and setting fixed times for messages are simple measures that have been shown to reduce stress in workplace trials. Professor Martens also recommends a less obvious step: warning colleagues when you do not wish to be disturbed. Interruptions, she points out, are a social problem, and a team that agrees on quiet hours protects everyone's concentration.

None of this requires abandoning technology, and most researchers have no wish to return to a world without instant communication, which has clear benefits for family life, safety and work. The question is who controls the timing. A tool that is used when we choose is a very different thing from one that decides for us. Attention, as one researcher puts it, is the only thing we spend that we can never earn back, and it may be worth treating it with at least as much care as money.
